strengths: The paper provides a unifying theoretical framework (Φ-normalized generalized attention, Definition 3.3) that covers softmax attention, linear attention, focused attention, MILA, and differential attention as special cases, and derives dispersion bounds for each (Table 1), which is a clean and pedagogically useful contribution.

The dispersion theorem (3.4) and its proof are rigorous under stated (compactness/boundedness) assumptions, and the paper carefully discusses when the assumption can fail (Remark 3.5) and connects the bound to prior work (Velickovic et al.).
The proposed architecture (window attention + global average, Eq. 13) is simple, interpretable, and computationally cheap (O(1) for the global term), and is well motivated by the dispersion analysis.

Empirical results are reported across multiple settings: ImageNet-1K classification at 224², finetuning at larger resolutions (384², 672², 768²), and COCO instance segmentation/detection, showing SEMA is competitive with or better than several strong recent Mamba-like and transformer baselines at similar parameter counts.
An ablation isolating the contribution of the averaging term is included, showing a measurable (if small) benefit.
Architectural and hyperparameter details are given in appendices (model config table, compute resources), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical dispersion result is explicitly stated to generalize Theorem 2.2 of Velickovic et al. (2024), and the proof technique closely follows that prior work; the novelty of the theory section is therefore incremental rather than foundational.

The link between the asymptotic (n→∞) dispersion result and the proposed fix (replacing the global attention term with a plain, query-independent uniform average, Eq. 13) is heuristic rather than rigorously justified; for the actual finite, moderate token counts used in vision (e.g., 49–196 per window/stage), it is unclear that discarding all query-dependence in the global term is a good approximation, and no empirical evidence (e.g., attention map visualizations or dispersion measurements before/after the fix) is provided to substantiate the motivating claim.

Experiments are restricted to tiny (~30M parameter) models only; despite "Scalable" being central to the title/claims, there is no evaluation of how SEMA behaves as model size grows, which is an important gap for validating scalability claims.
The improvement over the closest baseline (MILA-T) is small (83.7 vs 83.5 top-1, single run, no error bars/seeds reported), making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported gains.

Table 3 (higher-resolution finetuning) compares SEMA only against VMamba, omitting the more directly relevant comparison to MILA-T (the architecture SEMA is built on), which weakens the scalability argument.

COCO detection/segmentation results are mixed: in the 1x setting, MILA-T actually outperforms SEMA on some metrics (APb50, APm, APm50), yet the text characterizes SEMA as showing broad "superiority," which somewhat overstates the actual results.

The ablation study is minimal (only one comparison: with vs. without averaging); there is no ablation on window size choice, no comparison against alternative global-mixing strategies (e.g., learned/weighted averaging mentioned as future work), and no analysis explaining why averaging specifically outperforms other simple global aggregation choices.

Related work discussion under-engages with existing local-global hybrid vision architectures that similarly combine windowed/local attention with a global pooling or token mechanism (e.g., pyramid/global-token transformers), making it harder to assess how much of the empirical gain is attributable to the theoretical motivation versus a already-known architectural pattern.

Some claims in the text (e.g., describing MILA's forget-gate design as "mysterious," the ethics statement that datasets were "solely downloaded and evaluated by the university") are informal or vague and do not add rigor to the presentation.

strengths: Provides a unifying mathematical framework (generalized Φ-normalized attention) covering softmax, linear, focused, MILA, and differential attention, and proves a clean dispersion theorem showing these all converge to uniform attention as token count grows on a compact domain, plus a complementary probabilistic (weak-law-of-large-numbers based) version.

The proposed SEMA design (window attention + arithmetic averaging) is simple, well-motivated by the theory, and cheap to implement (O(1) global term), yielding a coherent story connecting theory to architecture.

Broad empirical validation across ImageNet-1K (T/S/B scales), COCO instance segmentation, and ADE20K semantic segmentation, with consistent (if modest) improvements over MILA and other Mamba-like/Mamba baselines at similar parameter counts.

Strong demonstration of robustness/scalability to larger input resolutions (384² to 1024²) both with and without finetuning, where SEMA notably outperforms VMamba, particularly at 1024² (7.3% gap without tuning).
Efficiency gains are demonstrated directly via wall-clock runtime comparisons against MILA, showing increasing speed advantage (up to ~33%) at higher resolutions, supporting the scalability claim.

Ablation studies isolate the contribution of the averaging term versus the value projection, and show (consistent with the theoretical narrative) that the averaging term's benefit grows with sequence length/resolution.
Reasonably transparent limitations section acknowledging the gap between asymptotic theory and finite practical settings, and the lack of extensive hyperparameter tuning due to compute constraints.
weaknesses: The practical relevance of the dispersion theorem is questionable: the paper's own measured dispersion rates on ImageNet (mean ~2.8x10^5) combined with modest token counts (e.g., 3136 tokens in stage 1) suggest the asymptotic dispersion regime is far from reached in practice, which is somewhat at odds with using this asymptotic result to justify the averaging design; the ablation shows the averaging term contributes only +0.2% at standard 224² resolution, undermining the centrality of the dispersion argument at typical operating scales.

Table 1 reports identical dispersion bounds (same generic formula) for softmax, linear, focused, and MILA attention, which appears uninformative/circular since it doesn't differentiate the practically distinct dispersion behaviors discussed in the text (e.g., linear attention disperses faster than softmax) â€” the table doesn't add insight beyond the general theorem.

The empirical gains over the main baseline (MILA) are quite modest at standard resolution (0.1-0.4% top-1 accuracy), and most results are based on single runs (acknowledged due to resource constraints), with no variance/significance reporting, making it hard to assess whether improvements are robust versus noise.

The large-resolution comparison in Table 3 is only against VMamba, not against MILA (the more directly comparable Mamba-like baseline); without finetuning MILA at large resolutions too, it is unclear how much of SEMA's advantage stems from the proposed attention change versus other architectural differences relative to VMamba's distinct macro-design.

The architectural contribution is somewhat incremental, essentially substituting window attention plus a global average for linear attention within the existing MILA macro-architecture, which limits methodological novelty beyond the theoretical framing.

The paper cites an apparently unpublished/future-dated companion work (Dayag et al., 2026) with results used to support generalizability claims (medical imaging), which cannot be independently verified and raises reproducibility/transparency concerns.

The compactness assumption underlying the main theorem, while defended as practically reasonable, is a strong simplification, and the authors themselves note the derived bounds are not tight, limiting the predictive/practical power of the theoretical results beyond a qualitative narrative.

strengths: The paper introduces a clean, unifying theoretical framework (generalized Φ-normalized attention) that subsumes softmax attention, linear attention, focused attention, and MILA, and proves a general dispersion theorem (Theorem 3.3) showing all of these asymptotically converge to uniform attention as the number of tokens grows. This nicely generalizes prior special cases (e.g., Veličković et al. 2025's Theorem 2.2) and gives a principled explanation for empirically observed phenomena (e.g., why linear attention in MILA behaves reasonably despite lacking a 'focusing' mechanism).

The architectural design (window attention + homogeneous/arithmetic averaging) is directly and transparently motivated by the theory: window attention avoids dispersion by keeping n fixed, while averaging matches the theoretically predicted asymptotic (uniform-weight) behavior of full attention in the large-n limit. This gives the method an unusually explainable rationale compared to typical ad hoc efficient-attention designs.

Strong and fairly comprehensive empirical validation: consistent improvements over MILA and VMamba across three model scales (T/S/B) on ImageNet-1K, plus downstream evaluation on COCO instance segmentation and ADE20K semantic segmentation, indicating the design generalizes beyond classification.

Particularly compelling large-resolution generalization experiments (384² to 1024²): SEMA degrades much more gracefully than VMamba without finetuning (e.g., 64.7% vs 57.4% at 1024²) and recovers with light finetuning, supporting the claimed scalability/robustness advantage motivated by the theory.
Efficiency gains are demonstrated directly (up to ~33% faster runtime than MILA at high resolutions), supporting the 'scalable and efficient' framing beyond just accuracy.

Reasonably thorough ablations (Tables 7-8) isolate the separate contributions of the value projection and the averaging term across resolutions, and the resolution-dependent trend of the averaging benefit (larger at higher resolution) is consistent with the paper's own dispersion-rate argument, strengthening the theory-practice link.
weaknesses: The core theoretical result, while a useful unification, is mathematically straightforward (continuity + compactness implies a bounded ratio, giving Θ(1/n) attention weights); the depth of the theoretical contribution is more in framing/generalization than in proof difficulty.

The asymptotic dispersion argument (n → ∞) has debatable practical relevance for the actual regimes used in the experiments, where token counts in later stages are small (e.g., 7×7=49 tokens in stage 4, where window and full attention coincide) — the paper itself acknowledges this softens the theory's applicability, and the ablation at standard 224² resolution shows the theoretically-motivated averaging term contributes only marginally (+0.2%) while most of the gain comes from an added value projection (extra capacity), which is a confound not fully disentangled from the dispersion-based design rationale.

Model comparisons (e.g., SEMA-T vs MILA-T/VMamba-T in Table 2) are not at strictly matched parameter counts or FLOPs; SEMA consistently uses slightly more parameters/FLOPs than baselines, making it harder to cleanly attribute accuracy gains to the theoretically motivated mechanism versus added capacity.

Most results are based on single training runs (acknowledged due to resource constraints), with no reported variance/error bars except an informal note of consistency for one setting, limiting statistical confidence in the reported gains, several of which are modest (e.g., 0.1-0.4 top-1 points in some comparisons).

The paper relies partly on results from an apparently concurrent/companion paper (Dayag et al., 2026, USEMA) with a 2026 publication date to support the generality of the averaging component on medical imaging tasks; this raises questions about independence of evidence and appropriateness of citing what appears to be unpublished/very recent work from what may be an overlapping author group.

Broader comparisons against other recent efficient/local-global hybrid attention mechanisms (beyond MILA and VMamba) are largely absent, so the significance of the proposed design relative to the wider landscape of efficient vision attention methods is not fully established.

The mechanistic novelty of the proposed local-global mixture (window attention plus global average) is fairly incremental relative to a long line of local+global efficient-attention designs (e.g., Swin, Longformer-style approaches); the main novelty is the theoretical justification rather than the mechanism itself.
